title: Queens Marked Diwali Early, With 2,000 at the Unisphere and a Wedding at Flushing
excerpt: Arts4All's free festival drew more than 2,000 people to the Unisphere on October 10, Flushing Town Hall staged its 12th annual festival on November 1, and the City Council's own Diwali celebration follows at City Hall on November 30.
body:
• Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8, 2026, and Diwali has been recognized as a New York City public school holiday since 2023.
  • More than 2,000 people attended the Arts4All Foundation's free Diwali and Navaratri festival at the Unisphere in Queens on October 10, according to the foundation.
  • Flushing Town Hall held its 12th annual Diwali Festival on November 1, built around an Indian wedding dance drama, with workshops, rangoli and food.
  • One official celebration is still ahead: the New York City Council hosts its Diwali, Deepavali and Bandi Chhor Divas celebration at City Hall on Monday, November 30, at 5:30 p.m., with RSVP through the Council's event page.

Queens did not wait for Diwali itself to celebrate it. Weeks before the festival's main day on Sunday, November 8, 2026, the borough's public celebrations had already drawn thousands of people, and the city's formal recognition of the holiday now runs from school calendars to a City Council celebration scheduled for later this month.

2,000 people at the Unisphere

More than 2,000 people attended the Arts4All Foundation's annual Diwali and Navaratri Festival and Parade on Saturday, October 10, at the World's Fair Unisphere in Queens, according to a press statement from the foundation reported by the South Asian Herald. Held under the theme "Unity through Light," the free event brought together community organizations, public officials, performers and families for cultural programs, a parade, and health and financial information services. The foundation said it was its largest gathering to date.

The foundation said it served more than 2,000 meals featuring dishes from different regions of India, and handed out 2,000 toys, 2,000 balloons and 1,000 chocolate coins to children. Activities included face painting, henna, rangoli artwork, yoga, books and games, and the festival offered free checkups and medical support from NYC Health + Hospitals/Elmhurst and Mount Sinai Hospital Queens, according to the statement.

"The gift of Diwali and Navaratri is the power to come together and illuminate our communities by lighting the Diya lamp of knowledge, truth, and hope."

— Dr. Sumita SenGupta, founder, Arts4All Foundation

Public figures listed as attending included New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, Assemblywoman Jessica González-Rojas, Councilmember Shekar Krishnan, Assemblymen Edward Braunstein and Steven Raga, and a representative of the Consulate General of India in New York. Raga presented SenGupta with a proclamation recognizing her community service, according to the statement. The parade began at sunset and the celebration concluded with a diya aarti ceremony.

Flushing Town Hall's Indian wedding

Three weeks later, Flushing Town Hall celebrated its 12th annual Diwali Festival on Sunday, November 1, from noon to 4 p.m. This year's theme was "The Indian Wedding." Workshops running from noon to 2 p.m. covered Indian dance steps, block printing, rangoli art, henna and Hindi calligraphy, and Queens Curry Kitchen sold Indian food and drinks through the afternoon, according to Flushing Town Hall.

At 2:15 p.m., Abha B. Roy and Srijan Dance Company performed a dance drama reenacting wedding customs including henna painting, the haldi ceremony, dances from different regions of India and the bride's farewell, with audiences welcoming the bridal party in a tassa drumming procession. Tickets were $20 for adults and $15 for member adults, with all children admitted free, at the venue at 137-35 Northern Blvd. in Flushing, Queens.

Recognition, and one date still to come

The celebrations sit inside a wider official recognition. Diwali, or Deepavali, takes its name from the Sanskrit phrase meaning "row of lights," and since 2023 it has been recognized as a New York City public school holiday, Flushing Town Hall noted in its festival announcement. This year the festival itself falls on a Sunday, November 8.

For readers who missed the Queens events, the city's own celebration is still upcoming. The New York City Council's Diwali, Deepavali and Bandi Chhor Divas Celebration is scheduled for Monday, November 30, 2026, in the Council Chambers at City Hall.

Plan Your Visit

  • Date: Monday, November 30, 2026
  • Time: 5:30 p.m. local time (doors open at 5:00 p.m.)
  • Venue: Council Chambers, New York City Hall
  • Admission: Not stated on the Council page — RSVP is through the official event page linked above.
  • Official page: NYC Council event page

Between a 2,000-person festival at the Unisphere, a wedding-themed afternoon in Flushing and a City Hall celebration still to come, New York's Diwali this year has been less a single day than a season — one the city now marks in its schools and its council chamber as well as its neighborhoods.
